title: Tribological Response and Surface Degradation Mechanisms of Heat Treated AISI 1040 Steel Under Dry Sliding: An Experimental and Statistical Modeling Study
abstract: Abstract The tribological performance and surface degradation behavior of medium carbon steels are strongly governed by microstructural evolution induced through heat treatment. In this study, the influence of annealing, normalizing, and oil quenching on the dry sliding wear behavior of AISI 1040 steel was systematically investigated under controlled tribological conditions. Pin on disc experiments were conducted in accordance with ASTM G99 using a hardened EN31 steel counter face, while varying applied load (20–60 N), sliding speed (0.5–1.5 m/s), and track diameter (0.04–0.08 m). Microstructural characterization revealed coarse ferrite–pearlite structures in annealed specimens, refined pearlite in normalized specimens, and martensitic transformation in oil quenched specimens, leading to progressive enhancement in load bearing capacity and hardness. 197, 203 and 227 HV were the measured hardness values for the annealed, normalized and oil quenched specimens respectively. The tribological response demonstrated a significant reduction in mass loss with increasing microstructural refinement, with oil quenched samples exhibiting superior wear resistance. The maximum measured mass loss decreased from 87 mg for annealed specimen, to 50 mg for normalized specimen, and to 45 mg for oil quenched specimen, showing a 48% reduction in mass loss. Surface degradation analysis using scanning electron microscopy indicated a transition in dominant wear mechanisms from severe abrasive–adhesive wear with delamination in annealed specimens to mild abrasive and oxidative wear in normalized specimens, and predominantly mild abrasive wear with limited plastic deformation in oil quenched specimens. Statistical analysis using ANOVA confirmed that applied load is the dominant factor influencing material removal across all heat-treated conditions, contributing up to 69.3% for annealed, 70.7% for normalized and 78.6% for oil quenched condition. Regression based predictive models and response surface optimization were developed to quantify the relationship between process parameters and wear performance. The regression models achieved R-sq values ranging from 90 to 94%, while the optimized wear loss values of 24, 7, and 1.5 mg closely agreed with the experimental values of 26, 7, and 1.9 mg. The results establish a clear correlation between heat treatment induced microstructural transformations, tribological behavior, and surface degradation mechanisms, providing a predictive framework for optimizing wear resistant performance of medium carbon steels in engineering applications. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Medium carbon steels are some of the most widely used structural materials in industry because of their balanced mechanical properties, machinability, availability and comparatively moderate cost. Among these steels, AISI 1040 is a plain medium carbon steel, with 0.37 to 0.44% carbon (C), which is known for its good strength, machinability and moderate welding properties, is widely used in industrial parts such as shafts, gears, axles, bolts, and other mechanical components subjected to repeated sliding contact. When in service, the steel surface experiences wear due to frictional sliding between the contacting surfaces, resulting in progressive removal of material from the surface. Continuous wear leads to surface degradation, deformation, loss of efficiency, and eventual failure of engineering components. Thus, improving the wear resistance of the structural steel remains an important objective in tribological engineering and materials processing studies.

In general, wear can be defined as the progressive removal of material from solid surfaces due to relative motion under load. During metallic sliding contacts, several wear mechanisms may occur, including adhesive wear, abrasive wear, oxidative wear, and delamination wear. Abrasive wear occurs when hard asperities or particles, known as abrasives, from a harder surface cut grooves into the softer surface. Adhesive wear occurs when the pressure between the contacting surfaces, sliding against each other, is high enough to cause localized plastic deformation, which leads to a phenomenon called bonding, wherein the detached material from the softer surface attaches itself to the harder surface, thus leaving a scratch on the softer material surface. Delamination wear occurs due to subsurface crack initiation and propagation, leading to sheet like removal of material. Oxidative wear occurs due to formation and removal of oxide films at the sliding interface [ 1 ]. The relationship between wear behavior and mechanical properties of a material can be explained by Archard wear law, which states that specific wear rate or volumetric wear rate (V) is directly proportional to the load applied (P) and the sliding distance (SD) and inversely proportional to the materials hardness. Thus, wear resistance (which is inversely proportional to specific wear rate) of a material can be improved by increasing the materials hardness through microstructural modifications [ 1 ].

For steels, especially medium carbon structural steels such as AISI 1040, one of the best methods to modify microstructure and improve their hardness is through heat treatment [ 2 ]. Through controlled heating and cooling cycles, the microstructure of AISI 1040 steel can be modified. Since phase composition has a strong influence on hardness and deformation characteristics, the microstructure of AISI 1040 steel plays a critical role in determining its wear behavior. Ferrite, which is a relatively softer phase with lower hardness, exhibits poor resistance to plastic deformation during sliding, thus resulting in higher wear rates. Pearlite phase, which consists of alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite phase, provides greater hardness and thus greater wear resistance than ferrite phase, due to the strengthening effect of cementite. Reduction in interlamellar spacing in pearlite phase, further increases hardness and improves wear resistance. Martensite phase forms during rapid cooling of austenite and thus possesses significantly higher hardness and wear resistance, due to its supersaturated structure [ 3 ]. Many investigations with regards to effect of heat treatment on hardness of steel have been carried out. Studies by Singh et al. [ 4 ] and Singh et al. [ 5 ], found that quenching plain medium carbon steels, such as AISI 1040 & 1045, resulted in a significantly higher hardness (30 to 50%) than annaling or normalizing heat treatment conditions. Investigations on the effects of different cooling media on hardness of AISI 1040 steel showed that increasing cooling severity increased martensite formation, thus increasing hardness [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. Studies on advanced heat treatment methods, such as dual phase heat treatment, reported that increasing intercritical process temperature, increased the martensite fraction in the ferrite-martensite duplex structure, thus improving hardness [ 9 ,  10 ]. These studies highlight the strong relationship between phase distribution and microstructure on hardness and other mechanical properties of AISI 1040 steel. Several other studies have also examined microstructure evolution and mechanical behavior of medium carbon steels under different heat treatment conditions, confirming that cooling rate, phase transformation, and microstructural refinement are the major factors that strongly influenced hardness and mechanical performance of steels [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 ,  16 – 17 ].

When it comes to studying the wear behavior of medium carbon structural steels, dry sliding wear using a pin on disc testing is the most commonly used method of wear testing, because the method provides controlled sliding conditions and reproducible wear measurements. In this method of wear testing, a cylindrical pin specimen is pressed against a rotating disc (of higher hardness) under a constant load. The relative sliding motion produces wear at the contact interface in between the cylindrical pin specimen and the rotating disc. The effects of parameters such as applied load, sliding speed, sliding distance and track diameter, on the wear rate, are generally studied by measuring the mass loss that the test specimen undergoes. Kumar et al. [ 18 ] and Kalwa et al. [ 19 ] who carried out dry sliding wear of medium carbon steel specimens on ceramic and alumina discs, found that wear rate increased significantly, 0.05 to 0.1 m³/Nm for alumina disc and 0.004 to 0.015 g/m 3  for ceramic disc, with increasing applied load due to higher contact stresses during sliding, with abrasive grooves and adhesion marks observed on the worn surfaces, indicating an abrasive adhesive wear domination during sliding. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) investigations of worn surfaces in several tribological studies [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 – 21 ] further revealed characteristic wear features such as ploughing grooves, plastic deformation marks, oxide debris layers, and delamination pits, which provide important evidence for identifying dominant wear mechanisms during dry sliding contact.

Microstructure refinement has a very significant influence on wear behavior of steels. Trivedi et al. [ 20 ], who studied the wear behavior of pearlitic railway wheel steel under dry sliding conditions, reported that refinement of pearlite lamellae increased hardness and significantly reduced wear rate of the steel. Analyzing comparative tribological studies, that investigated the wear behavior of EN8 (AISI 1040), EN9, and EN24 steels, it was observed that steels with higher hardenability, due to presence of higher carbon content and alloying elements such as Nickel (Ni), Chromium (Cr) and Molybdenum, had comparatively lower wear rate and higher wear resistance than plain medium carbon steels, as alloying resulted in refinement of ferrite-pearlite phase colonies, leading to increase hardness [ 21 ,  22 ]. Similarly, Bassam Ali Ahmed [ 23 ], who studied the effect of different quenching media on dry sliding wear behavior of medium carbon steel, reported that water-quenched specimens exhibited lower wear rates, due to formation of harder martensitic microstructures.

Surface treatment methods such as boronizing, which forms FeB and Fe 2 B layers on the steel surface, have been known to significantly improve the surface hardness of medium carbon steels, thus improving wear resistance, while carbide coatings such as Niobium Carbide (NbC) have also been reported to improve wear resistance by providing a hard protective surface layer that suppresses abrasive damage [ 3 ,  24 ]. Similarly, electroless Ni–P coatings subjected to heat treatment, demonstrated that heat treatment improved tribological behavior due to precipitation hardening that increased coating hardness and reduced wear rate [ 25 ]. Additional investigations on wear behavior of steels [ 26 ,  27 ,  28 ,  29 – 30 ]. collectively emphasize the importance of hardness, microstructure, and surface modification in improving wear performance of medium carbon steels.

With respect to statistical analysis of dry sliding wear behavior of AISI 1040 steel, Agrawal and Mukhopadhyay [ 27 ], carried out optimization study of wear rate and coefficient of friction (COF) of AISI 1040 steel using grey relational analysis, reported that at a load of 50 N, 0.5 m/s sliding speed and 700 m sliding distance gave the best combination of wear (0.4571 g/Nm) and COF (0.620), with load being the major contributing (51%) factor. Kalwa et al. [ 19 ], developed an ordinary least square method to predict the wear rate of EN8 carbon steels, for varying sliding speed, sliding time and load conditions. Prasanta Sahoo [ 25 ], who studied the wear behavior of electroless Ni-P coatings and carried out optimization wear parameters using Taguchi method, reported that heat treatment temperature and cooling rate were the main factors affecting wear rate.

Dry sliding wear tests were conducted against hardened EN31 steel counter face disc as per ASTM G99-17 standards [ 31 ], while varying applied load, sliding speed, and track diameter. The effects of applied load, sliding speed and track diameter on mass loss and wear rate were also studied and optimized using statistical analysis tools such as ANOVA, regression and response surface optimization.

Although the general trend of annealed, normalized, and quenched steels showing progressively improved wear resistance is well established, limited studies have quantitatively connected heat-treatment-induced microstructural changes in AISI 1040 steel with dry sliding mass loss, specific wear rate, SEM-based wear mechanisms, and predictive statistical models under a common experimental framework. The novelty of the present study lies in integrating heat-treatment response, pin-on-disc wear performance, SEM-based surface degradation analysis, ANOVA-based factor ranking, regression modelling, and response surface optimization for AISI 1040 steel. This approach not only compares the wear behavior of annealed, normalized, and oil-quenched conditions but also identifies the dominant wear-controlling parameters and provides predictive equations for estimating mass loss within the selected tribological window. The objective of this investigation is to analyze how heat treatment-induced microstructural changes influence the wear behavior of AISI 1040 steel under controlled tribological conditions and the effects of wear parameters on wear rate, while identifying the dominant wear parameter and wear mechanisms for each heat treatment condition, and developing a predictive model for wear performance.

paragraphs: The dry sliding wear test specimens were prepared as per ASTM G99-17 standard [ 31 ] dimensions, as shown in Fig.  1 .

sections.heading: Heat Treatment Process
paragraphs: The aim of the prior heat treatment was to obtain the superior combination of hardness and impact energy. Accordingly, the heat treatment parameters, namely temperature and holding time are selected based on the prior reported study [ 12 ]. Annealing heat treatment was carried out using conventional furnace cooling, while normalizing treatment adopted air cooling. Hardening treatment was carried out using the SAE 40 engine oil as quenchant. Table  2  provides the heat treatment parameters used for each treatment along with the results obtained for the hardness and impact energy for the heat treated samples, while Fig.  2  represents the heat treatment cycle.

Fig. 2 Heat treatment cycle

The respective hardness of the specimens, for each heat treatment conditions, as shown in Table  2 , was measured on a Vickers microhardness testing machine, at an applied load of 30 kgf for a dwell time of 15 s, available at Advanced Material Testing Laboratory, MIT, Manipal.

sections.heading: Pin on Disc Dry Sliding Wear Test
paragraphs: After heat treatment, dry sliding wear test was carried out on a DUCOM TR20 NEO pin on disc wear and friction testing machine, as shown in Fig.  3 , at the advanced material testing (AMT) lab, MIT, Manipal. An EN31 hardened carbon steel material wear disc, of 697 HV hardness, was used for the wear test, so that hardness of the disc material would be more than hardness of heat treated AISI 1040 steel wear test specimens.
Fig. 3 Wear testing machine
The test parameter ranges for the dry sliding wear test, are as tabulated in Table  3 . A fixed sliding distance of 3600 m was maintained for all conditions.
Table 3 Wear test parameters Factors Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Load (N) 20 40 60 Track diameter (m) 0.04 0.06 0.08 Sliding speed (m/s) 0.5 1.0 1.5 Sliding distance (m) 3600

The wear test parameter ranges, as shown in Table  3 , were selected based on previous tribological studies on medium carbon steels [ 18 ,  27 ], along with the operational limitations of the pin on disc wear testing machine. During preliminary experimentation, it was observed that for the respective steel specimen, the machine could only operate efficiently at a maximum load of 100 N and a sliding speed of 800 rpm. The operational track diameter range of the counterface disc was from 0.02 to 0.1 m. Thus, the selected parameter ranges provide sufficient variation to evaluate the influence of wear parameters under dry sliding conditions.

To measure the mass loss Δm (in mg) for each test condition, the mass of the respective specimen was measured on a JEE-LIT BH-JY series electronic balance, with a 1 mg least count, before and after testing. sections.heading: SEM and Statistical Analysis
paragraphs: SEM imaging of the wear surface was done on EVO MA18 SEM analyzer, at CAIF, MIT, Manipal. Amongst load, sliding speed and track diameter, to identify which of these wear parameters had the most significant effect on mass loss, statistical analysis was carried out using general linear modelling, and ANOVA at 5% significance level was obtained. Regression models were developed to predict mass loss as a function of load, sliding speed and track diameter. A custom response surface design was defined and analyzed, keeping load, sliding speed and track diameter as continuous factors and mass loss as response. Response surface optimization, a method used to develop predictive models and determine the optimum wear conditions, was performed with mass loss set to minimize. Finally, main effect plots were generated to visualize individual influence of each wear test parameter on mass loss.

Each experimental condition was evaluated based on the available measured response from the Taguchi L9 design. Since full replicate testing was not carried out for every condition, the statistical analysis is interpreted within the limitations of the experimental design. The ANOVA results are used to identify the relative influence of track diameter, load, and sliding speed on mass loss, while the regression equations are considered valid only within the selected experimental range. Future studies with repeated trials, confidence intervals, and residual normality validation would further improve the robustness of the predictive models.

It is important to note that the present microstructural interpretation is primarily based on SEM observation and hardness response. Quantitative phase fraction analysis using XRD or EBSD was not performed in the present work. Therefore, phase identification, particularly in the oil-quenched condition, is discussed qualitatively and correlated with hardness and wear behavior. Future work may include XRD/EBSD-based phase quantification, retained austenite estimation, and microhardness mapping to provide stronger confirmation of transformation products.

sections.heading: Analysis of as Received Specimen
paragraphs: The SEM image as shown in Fig.  4 , shows the surface of as received AISI 1040 specimen, before wear test. The microstructure of as received AISI 1040 steel, shows fine colony pearlites with ferrite grains. The size of the pearlite colony is finer than annealed and coarser than normalized condition. This microstructure correlates well with measured hardness of 200 HV.
Fig. 4 SEM image of as received AISI 1040 steel

The as received specimen was subjected to dry sliding wear test at 0.06 m track diameter, 40 N load and 1 m/s sliding speed. The mass loss, wear and specific wear rate obtained are as tabulated in Table  5 .

Table 5 Wear test results of as received AISI 1040 steel Track diameter (m) Load ( N ) Sliding speed (m/s) Mass loss Δm (mg) Wear 10 − 9  (kg/m) Specific wear rate 10 − 14  (m 3 /Nm) 0.06 40 1 41 11.4 3.6
Fig. 5 SEM images of as received AISI 1040 steel subjected to wear

The worn surface of as received AISI 1040 steel, as shown in Fig.  5 , tested at 40 N load, 1 m/s sliding speed, 0.06 m track diameter, and 60 min sliding time, shows long, continuous grooves aligned with sliding direction, accompanied by plastic flow ridges and localized smearing, confirming dominant two body abrasive wear with secondary adhesive contribution. The moderate groove depth and absence of large delamination pits or brittle spallation indicate stable ductile ploughing rather than severe surface fracture, which is consistent with the estimated mass loss of approximately 41 mg, corresponding to a wear rate of 11.4 × 10 –9 kg/m and a specific wear rate of 3.6 × 10–14 m³/Nm under this condition, as tabulated in Table  5 .

sections.heading: Wear and Statistical Analysis of Annealed AISI 1040 Steel
paragraphs: The SEM image of annealed AISI 1040 wear test specimen prior to wear test, as shown in Fig.  6 , shows a microstructure consisting of large colony coarse pearlite with ferrite grains. The pearlite colony is coarser than that of as received specimen. The microstructure correlates well with a hardness value of 197 HV, as shown in Table  2 .
Fig. 6 SEM image of annealed AISI 1040 steel
The mass loss, wear and wear rate results for annealed AISI 1040 steel specimens subjected to dry sliding wear, are as shown below in Table  6 .
Fig. 7 SEM images of annealed AISI 1040 steel subjected to wear

The worn surface of annealed AISI 1040 specimen, as shown in Fig.  7 , shows dense wide grooves aligned with the sliding direction, accompanied by extensive plastic smearing and fragmented debris patches, indicating a dominant abrasive ploughing with significant adhesive contribution. Local surface tearing, shallow delamination pockets, and discontinuous tribo-oxide compaction appear along the wear track, reflecting repeated fracture and removal of mechanically mixed layers under sustained contact stress. These surface features correlate well with measured increase in mass loss with increasing load and speed as tabulated in Table  6 , where mass loss rises from 26 mg at 0.04 m / 20 N / 0.5 m/s to 87 mg at 0.08 m / 60 N / 1.5 m/s. The corresponding increase in wear from 7.2 to 24.2 × 10  –9  kg/m and specific wear rate from 4.6 to 5.1 × 10 –14  m 3 /Nm, shows a clear transition from mild abrasive wear at lower severity to a more severe abrasive–adhesive wear regime at higher contact severity, as reflected in the SEM morphology.
The ANOVA results of mass loss for annealed AISI 1040 steel are as tabulated in Table  7 .

Table 7 ANOVA results of mass loss for annealed AISI 1040 steel Source DF Adj SS Adj MS F-Value P -Value % Contribution Track diameter (m) 2 771.56 385.78 20.19 0.047 27.5 Load (N) 2 1942.89 971.44 50.83 0.019 69.3 Sliding speed (m/s) 2 50.89 25.44 1.33 0.429 Error 2 38.22 19.11 Total 8 2803.56
Fig. 8 Main effects plot of mass loss for annealed AISI 1040 steel

The ANOVA results presented in Table  7  indicate that load is the most significant factor affecting mass loss during dry sliding wear. Influence of load on mass loss of annealed AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen is nearly 69.3%, while track diameter has a secondary impact of 27.5%. Since P-values of track diameter (0.047) and load (0.019) are both lower than 0.05, both factors are found to be statistically significant, while sliding speed with P-value of 0.429 was found to be statistically insignificant. This proved that, for annealed AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen, material removal is governed by load induced wear deformation. The main effects plot shown in Fig.  8 , shows that, when track diameter increased from 0.04 to 0.08 m, mass loss increased by 22 mg, while increase in load from 20 to 60 N led to a 36 mg increase in mass loss. Increase in sliding speed from 0.5 to 1.5 m/s resulted in a 2 mg decrease in mass loss.
The regression analysis of wear data from Table  7  yielded the regression Eq. ( 5 ) for mass loss;

Given the R-sq value of 92.56%, regression Eq. ( 5 ) can be considered reliable for predicting the mass loss of annealed AISI 1040 steel respectively, for the dry sliding wear conditions examined in this study.

sections.heading: Wear and Statistical Analysis of Normalized AISI 1040 Steel
paragraphs: The SEM image of normalized AISI 1040 wear test specimen prior to wear test, as shown in Fig.  9 , shows a microstructure consisting of very fine pearlite colony with ferrite grains. The pearlite colony is finer than that of the pearlite colony of as received and annealed specimens. The microstructure correlates well with the hardness of 203 HV, as shown in Table  2 .
Fig. 9 SEM image of normalized AISI 1040 steel
The mass loss, wear and wear rate results for normalized AISI 1040 steel specimens subjected to dry sliding wear, are as shown in Table  8 .
Fig. 10 SEM images of normalized AISI 1040 steel subjected to wear

The worn surface of normalized AISI 1040 steel, as shown in Fig.  10 , exhibits parallel grooves aligned with the sliding direction, mixed with compacted debris patches and localized surface smearing. Compared to annealed worn surface (Fig.  7 ), the grooves are narrower and more uniform, and large scale delamination is absent, due to the finer ferrite–pearlite microstructure produced by normalizing. The presence of mixed layers and fragmented oxide debris suggests a mixed abrasive-oxidative wear mechanism, rather than purely severe abrasion. The surface characteristics correlate well with the measured wear data, as shown in Table  8 , were mass loss increases from 7 mg at 0.04 m/20 N to 50 mg at 0.08 m/60 N, while remaining consistently lower than annealed steel under similar conditions. The corresponding rise in wear from 1.9 to 13.9 × 10  –9  kg/m and specific wear rate from 1.2 to 3 × 10 –14  m 3 /Nm, shows a transition from mild abrasive wear at lower load to a moderately severe abrasive–adhesive regime at higher load and wear severity. Overall, it was observed that normalization enhanced wear resistance by refining the ferrite–pearlite microstructure, promoting strain hardening and partial oxide stability, which delayed the onset of severe delamination-dominated wear while maintaining controlled material removal across the tested conditions.
The ANOVA results for mass loss are as tabulated in Table  9 .

Table 9 ANOVA results of mass loss for normalized AISI 1040 steel Source DF Adj SS Adj MS F-Value P -Value % Contribution Track diameter (m) 2 389.56 194.78 11.17 0.082 23.3 Load (N) 2 1182.89 591.44 33.90 0.029 70.7 Sliding speed (m/s) 2 64.89 32.44 1.86 0.350 3.9 Error 2 34.89 17.44 2 Total 8 1672.22
Fig. 11 Main effects plot of mass loss for normalized AISI 1040 steel

The ANOVA results presented in Table  9  indicate that load is the most significant factor affecting mass loss during dry sliding wear. Influence of load on mass loss of normalized AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen is nearly 70.7%. Load, with a P-value of 0.029, was found to be statistically significant, while track diameter and sliding speed, with P-values of 0.082 and 0.350, were statistically insignificant. This proved that, for normalized AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen, material removal is governed by load induced wear deformation. The main effects plot shown in Fig.  11 , shows that mass loss increased by 16 mg with increase in track diameter from 0.04 to 0.08 m, while increase in load from 20 to 60 N led to a 28 mg increase in mass loss. Increase in sliding speed from 0.5 to 1.5 m/s only resulted in a small increase of 5 mg in mass loss.
The regression analysis of normalized AISI 1040 steel yielded the regression Eq. ( 6 ) for mass loss;

Given the R-sq value of 94.18%, regression Eq. ( 6 ) can be considered reliable for predicting the mass loss of normalized AISI 1040 steel respectively, for the dry sliding wear conditions examined in this study.

sections.heading: Wear and Statistical Analysis of Oil Quenched AISI 1040 Steel
paragraphs: The SEM image of the oil-quenched AISI 1040 specimen, shown in Fig.  12 , indicates a hardened microstructure with features consistent with partial transformation after oil quenching. However, the measured hardness of 227 HV suggests that the structure should not be interpreted as fully martensitic. The relatively moderate hardness may be attributed to the oil-quenching severity, section size effect, possible incomplete austenitization or incomplete martensitic transformation, and the presence of ferrite/pearlite along with transformed products.

The mass loss, wear and wear rate results for oil quenched AISI 1040 steel specimens subjected to dry sliding wear, are as shown in Table  10 .

Fig. 13 SEM images of oil quenched AISI 1040 steel subjected to wear

The SEM image of oil quenched AISI 1040 steel (Fig.  13 ) shows relatively shallow, narrow grooves aligned with the sliding direction, with a largely smooth surface and limited evidence of plastic deformation. The grooves are discontinuous and less pronounced than those observed in annealed and normalized conditions, while compacted debris and large delamination features are largely absent. The surface looks more uniform, with reduced delamination and localized oxide compaction, reflecting the higher hardness and improved load-bearing capacity of martensitic microstructure. The wear data (Table  10 ), shows that at 20 N–0.04 m, mass loss is around 8 mg, corresponding to a very low wear of 2.2 × 10  –9  kg/m and wear rate of 1.4 × 10 –14  m 3 /Nm. While at higher loads of 60 N–0.08 m, mass loss increases to 45 mg at a wear of 12.5 × 10  –9  kg/m, at a specific wear rate of 2.7 × 10 -14  m 3 /Nm. The mass loss values are significantly lower than annealed and normalized specimens for similar conditions, thus showing that oil quenching improves the dry sliding wear resistance of AISI 1040 steel by restricting plastic deformation and delaying transition from mild abrasive to a severe abrasive adhesive wear regime.
The ANOVA results for mass loss are as tabulated in Table  11 .

The ANOVA results presented in Table  11  indicate that load is the most significant factor affecting mass loss during dry sliding wear. Influence of load on mass loss of oil quenched AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen is nearly 78.6%. Out of the three factors, only load was found to be statistically significant since its P-value was found to be lower than 0.05. This proved that, for oil quenched AISI 1040 steel wear test specimen, material removal is governed by load induced wear deformation. The main effects plot shown in Fig.  14 , shows that mass loss increased by 11 mg with increase in track diameter from 0.04 to 0.08 m, while increase in load from 20 to 60 N led to a 26 mg increase in mass loss. sections.heading: Response Surface Optimization Results
paragraphs: A response surface optimization was carried out on the wear results obtained in Tables  6 ,  8 , and  10 , for identifying the optimal wear test conditions that yielded the lowest mass loss for each of the heat treated conditions. This optimization approach established process parameters that simultaneously meet the desired criteria for multiple responses. The results, as summarized in Table  12 , highlight the wear parameter combinations that provided the lowest mass loss for each heat treatment conditions for AISI 1040 steel.

Table 12 Response surface optimization results Heat treatment Track diameter (m) Load ( N ) Sliding speed (m/s) Mass loss (mg) optimized Annealed 0.05 20 0.5 24 Normalized 0.04 20 0.5 7 Oil quenched 0.04 20 1.5 1.5

The response surface optimization results, as shown in Table  12 , with the goal of minimizing mass loss, showed low load conditions as favorable conditions for all heat treated steels, with oil-quenched conditions consistently showing the lowest optimized mass loss. Optimized mass loss decreased from 24 mg in the annealed condition to 7 mg after normalizing and further to 1.5 mg after oil quenching, closely matching the experimental values of 26, 7, and 1.9 mg, which confirmed good model reliability. The small deviation between optimized and experimental values indicated that the response surface model captured the dominant wear-controlling factors effectively. Overall, the response surface analysis confirmed that wear resistance improved systematically with increasing microstructural hardness and load-bearing capacity, and that the optimization results are physically consistent with the observed wear mechanisms and experimental trends [ 18 ].

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study established a clear relationship between the different heat treatments, microstructures, and dry sliding wear behavior of AISI 1040 steel. Quantitative wear data, statistical analysis, and SEM observations consistently showed that increasing hardness and microstructural stability reduced mass loss and delayed the transition from mild to severe wear. The following conclusions were drawn based on the results obtained:

Heat treatment strongly influenced dry sliding wear behavior of AISI 1040 steel. Load was the most dominant parameter affecting mass loss for all heat treatment conditions, with a 69.3% contribution for annealing, 70.7% for normalizing and 78.6% for oil quenching. Annealing resulted in the lowest wear resistance, with specific wear rate ranging from 4.6 to 7.3 × 10 –14  m³/Nm, due to severe plastic deformation and delamination. Normalizing, with specific wear rate ranging from 1.2 to 5 × 10 –14  m³/Nm, showed improved wear resistance due to refinement of the ferrite–pearlite structure and enhancing strain hardening. Oil quenching, with specific wear rate ranging from 1.1 to 2.7 × 10 –14  m³/Nm, provided the best wear resistance by suppressing plastic flow and delaying delamination. SEM images showed clear wear features across all heat treated AISI 1040 steel surfaces. Annealed and as received specimens showed wider grooves, plastic smearing, debris patches, surface tearing, and local delamination. Normalized states showed finer parallel grooves with compacted oxide debris and mixed layers, while oil quenched states showed shallow grooves, smooth tracks, micro polishing, limited debris, and absence of severe delamination. Even though there was very little difference between hardness values for the as received, annealed and normalized specimens (± 3 HV), their wear behavior differed. This showed that hardness alone is insufficient to explain the observed wear behavior, thus proving that the effect that respective heat treatment has on the morphology and microstructure of the steel also have significant effect on load distribution, plastic deformation, crack initiation, and debris formation during wear.

Thus, the findings of this study help in providing a practical approach for selecting the suitable heat treatment conditions for AISI 1040 steel undergoing dry sliding wear. Annealed AISI 1040 steel is suitable for applications requiring good machinability with lower resistance to wear, while normalized AISI 1040 steel, with a balanced combination of strength and wear resistance, are suitable for general engineering components. Whereas oil quenched AISI 1040 steel, because of the comparatively higher hardness, wear resistance and reduced material loss, is best suited for wear critical components that are subjected to repeated sliding contact, such as shafts, gears, pins, rollers, and automotive components. The developed statistical models can be helpful for selecting appropriate operating parameters to minimize wear and improve the components service life.
